Adult female Sichuan torrent frogs attain a maximum snout–vent length of 7.15 cm [Li = 7.15 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the genus Amolops. In contrast, adult males are distinctly smaller, achieving an ultimate snout–vent length of 5.66 cm [Li = 5.66 cm], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is widespread among ranid frogs and is often linked to differential reproductive investment. The wet weight of a newly hatched tadpole, which emerges from the gelatinous egg mass following eclosion, is approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams]. This minute mass reflects the modest energy reserves contained within the yolk-laden egg and constrains the early survival of the free-swimming larva. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C], the age at birth, meaning the time from oviposition to hatching, has been recorded as 12 days [ab = 12 days], a developmental duration that is notably prolonged at such low temperatures compared to many lowland congeners.

The maximum lifespan reported for Amolops mantzorum is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], based on mark-recapture studies conducted in montane streams at a mean annual water temperature of 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a frog of this body size and likely reflects the slow life-history pace imposed by the cold, oligotrophic environments it inhabits. Following metamorphosis, the timing of sexual maturation diverges between the sexes. This measurement represents the body size at which the tail is resorbed and the gills are replaced by lungs, marking the shift from an aquatic to a terrestrial mode of life. Upon completing this morphological transformation, the recently metamorphosed juvenile, or froglet, weighs considerably more than the hatchling, as it has accumulated somatic tissue during the actively growing larval phase. However, the body mass of adult females substantially exceeds that of the juveniles. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 37.3 grams [Wwi = 37.3 grams], a mass that is more than double that of adult males, which attain a peak body weight of 18.5 grams [Wwi = 18.5 grams]. This pronounced difference in asymptotic mass between the sexes is a direct consequence of the female's need to accommodate and provision a large clutch of yolked oocytes.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized under laboratory conditions at 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C], where females have been observed to produce approximately 3730 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3730 eggs per year]. This value represents the maximum reproductive rate, combining the size of individual clutches with the frequency of spawning events over the course of a single breeding season. The production of such a large number of offspring is typical of many stream-breeding ranids that experience high levels of larval mortality. The adult females that achieve the 37.3 gram [Wwi = 37.3 gram] body weight are presumably those that can allocate the greatest proportion of their acquired energy to gametogenesis. The annual fecundity of approximately 3730 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3730 eggs per year] is a substantial investment, one that is energetically feasible only because the frogs exploit the abundant aquatic insect prey found in their torrential habitat during the warm summer months.

In addition to the life-history traits already discussed, ecological comparisons with related species provide context. Many congeners in the genus Amolops share similar habitat preferences for rocky, fast-flowing streams in montane regions, where their specialized ventral suction discs allow them to cling to submerged surfaces. The low temperature of 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C] that characterizes their high-elevation environment exerts a strong constraint on all metabolic and developmental rates, effectively prolonging the incubation period and the time to sexual maturation relative to lowland frogs. The recorded lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] is consistent with the maximum longevities reported for other ranids from cold climates, where slow growth and late reproduction are favored by stable, resource-limited conditions at a temperature of 6.5 °C [T = 6.5 °C]. Furthermore, the dispersal of recently metamorphosed juveniles away from natal streams is thought to be limited, leading to relatively high levels of population structure across the fragmented watersheds of the Hengduan Mountains.
